newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland paves way to return some Jewish property.
newsitem.headline: Poland paves way to return some Jewish property.

text.p: Poland's parliament on Thursday approved a bill on state relations with Jewish communities, which will allow the nine tiny congregations to recover some properties lost during and after the World War Two Holocaust.

Nazi German invaders robbed and murdered most of Poland's 3.5 million Jews during the war and communal properties such as synagogues, schools and ritual bath-houses were then taken over by Poland's post-war communist authorities.

The bill, which easily cleared the lower house but must still pass through the Senate to become law, will provide a legal framework for the surviving congregations, grouping 3,000 to 5,000 Jews, to claim some of these back.
Pawel Wildstein, head of the Union of Jewish Communities in Poland, cautiously welcomed the bill but said it had flaws.

"The Union and I are fairly pleased that after 800 years of our existence on Polish soil we have got a basic document like this law regulating relations between the state and the Jews," Wildstein told Reuters.
He criticised some aspects of the bill, including a clause preventing claims on property which has already been sold or passed on to third parties such as private individuals.
The government estimates that there are some 1,100 cemeteries, 350 prayer houses, 28 funeral homes, 27 schools, as well as hospitals and other sites that once belonged to Jewish groups.
Some Polish critics of the bill argued it might allow the tiny Jewish minority to inherit a huge legacy which it could not use, while depriving current occupants of such assets.

The cash-starved Jewish congregations expect to reclaim some properties and to derive income from others to pay bills, provide social welfare for the old or look after cemeteries -- sacred in Jewish tradition -- which have fallen into ruin or been vandalised in the absence of anyone to tend them.
Wildstein ridiculed talk that the property Jewish bodies could potentially reclaim represented huge fortunes.

"These are half-destroyed remnants of prayer house walls, these are 1,064 cemeteries, knocked down, wrecked, profaned. Even if we just tried to put walls up around these cemeteries...the money would not pay for one half," he said.

Jewish organisations abroad, who have long been pressing the Polish government to settle property issues left over from the Holocaust and the communist era, were much more strongly critical of the bill.

"This is a minimalistic bill and does not give back the Jewish communities the possession of properties that belonged to them before 1939," said Naphtali Lavie, vice-chairman of the Israel-based World Jewish Restitution Organisation (WJRO).

Lavie said it actually guaranteed that only those buildings now in use by the nine congregations would be regained, but Polish government officials say the scope would in fact be much wider than that.
The bill is one of several voted on on Thursday concerning small religious minorities whose status is still unregulated, unlike that of the Roman Catholic Church which was settled years ago.
It does not address private property -- an issue Poland plans to settle with a wide bill on reprivatisation treating all citizens alike, irrespective of ethnic origin.
Jewish organisations abroad say this bill, which would compensate only resident citizens, would discriminate against the many Polish Jews who emigrated or fled the country during and after the war.
